name: Iris Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site joiner for Northgate Construction, which builds most of the apartment blocks in our town. Right now we're on a seven-storey block by the canal, and I do the first fix, the timber grounds and door linings, and then I come back to hang the fire doors. I also keep an eye on the two apprentices, Ellie and Jordan, because someone did that for me thirty years ago. I like the order of it, floor by floor, door by door. The stairs before the lift goes in are what wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You look after two apprentices. What's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Yusuf drives a taxi, nights mostly, and he's at the mosque more than I am these days. Our daughter Sana works in a pharmacy and our youngest, Bilal, is in the second year of an electrical apprenticeship, which I'm very proud of. Money's thin, we've got maybe three weeks saved, Yusuf's taxi is on a loan. Northgate's the only big builder in town, so if they don't want you, you're driving an hour for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to work. To the apprentices I'd say, see, the trade's still here, keep learning it properly. I'm on a family chat and that's it, I'd send a thumbs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It suits me. Bilal's apprenticeship stays worth something, my job stays the same, Yusuf keeps driving. The only problem is the money's still tight, but that's always been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northgate and keep teaching Ellie and Jordan. I already use one of those AI apps now and then to check a fire door rule when the paperwork's confusing, I'd keep doing that. And I'd keep trying to get Yusuf's taxi loan paid down a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, glad even. Life as it is, which is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI app to check fire door rules. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jordan showed me. The fire door rules change every couple of years and the booklet is thick and badly written. I typed in my question and it told me the gap under the door had to be smaller than I thought. I checked with the site manager and it was right, so now I use it when I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does teaching the apprentices matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man called Derek taught me when nobody else would take a girl on site in 1986. He let me make mistakes on cheap timber. I owe him, and the way you pay that back is to do it for the next one.

S0.say: Good, now let's get back to work, and the trade's still here so keep learning it properly. I'd send a thumbs up to the family chat.
S0.think: It suits me, because my son's apprenticeship keeps its worth and nothing changes at home. Money's still tight, but it always has been.
S0.do: Keeps working at Northgate and keeps teaching her two apprentices. Uses an AI app now and then to check fire door rules, and tries to pay down her husband's taxi loan faster.
S0.feel: Calm and glad, because life as it is feels like enough.
S0.quote: He let me make mistakes on cheap timber.
S0.fieldNote: Iris defines herself partly through passing on the trade, as someone once did for her. She uses AI occasionally but checks it with the site manager, which fits her steady approach. Her calm here rests heavily on her son's apprenticeship holding its value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has its new tools, and you learn them like you learned the old ones. To the apprentices I'd say learn the new stuff and the old stuff. I wouldn't say the government should do anything, firms should look after their own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Yusuf than me. Joinery on a site is fiddly, every frame is a little out. But driving a taxi, that's the thing everyone says the self-driving cars will take first, and he's 61 with a loan on the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few of the others had tried them, I'd learn whatever new tools Northgate brings in, the scanners or the robot that marks out walls. I'd sit down with Yusuf and work out how to clear the taxi loan in two years instead of four, even if it means no trip to see my sister this year. And I'd keep pushing the apprentices to get every certificate going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own work so much, more for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should look after their own people. What would that look like at Northgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train the people who've been loyal before you hire new ones. I've been there nineteen years. If they bring in a robot, they should teach me to run it before they advertise for some lad from the city. That's what a decent firm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Yusuf go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the cars can't drive in snow, and I'd say that's not a plan, that's weather. We'd argue, then he'd make tea and agree. He's stubborn, but he's not stupid.

S1.say: Every generation has new tools and you learn them like the old ones. Firms, not government, should look after their own people.
S1.think: I'm more worried about Yusuf than me, since self-driving cars are expected to take taxi work first. He's 61 with a loan on the car, while site joinery is fiddly enough to be safer.
S1.do: Learns Northgate's new tools once a few others have tried them, such as scanners or wall-marking robots. Plans with Yusuf to clear the taxi loan in two years instead of four, skipping a family trip, and pushes the apprentices to collect every certificate.
S1.feel: Uneasy, less for her work than for the household.
S1.quote: He'd say the cars can't drive in snow, and I'd say that's not a plan, that's weather.
S1.fieldNote: Her household's real exposure is her husband's taxi, not her joinery, and she sees that clearly. She expects loyalty from her employer rather than help from government, in line with her traditional outlook. She'd adopt tools once others have proven them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and families will have to pull together. I'd tell people at the mosque and at work to look after each other. I don't want handouts, but I'd say firms should do right by their workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be very bad for us. I'd be 60, Yusuf 63, both our jobs hit at once, three weeks of money and a taxi loan. And Bilal would just be finishing his apprenticeship into a world where robots do the wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those two years I'd work every hour Northgate gives and put away what I can. Yusuf and I would cut right down, and we might sell the taxi and pay off the loan before it's worth nothing. I'd do kitchen fitting at weekends for people from the mosque, cash, and if it got bad, we'd lean on my brother, who has a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep, and I'd pray for strength.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Bilal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish the apprenticeship anyway, because a finished thing is worth more than a half one. But I wouldn't know what to tell him after that. That's the hardest part, being his mother and not having an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. If the government offered income support, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to choosing between that and losing the flat, yes, I would, and I wouldn't like it. I'd go to my brother first, that's what family's for. But I'm not going to let pride put us on the street.

S2.say: It's come too fast and families will have to pull together. I don't want handouts, but firms should do right by their workers.
S2.think: It'd be very bad, with both our jobs hit at once, three weeks of money and a taxi loan. My son would finish his apprenticeship into a world where robots do the wiring.
S2.do: Works every available hour in the two years before and saves what she can. Plans to sell the taxi to clear the loan, fits kitchens at weekends for cash, and would lean on her brother first and government only if they faced losing the flat.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and praying for strength.
S2.quote: That's the hardest part, being his mother and not having an answer.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits her household twice, through her job and her husband's taxi, and her son's future on top. She'd turn to family and community first and admits she'd accept state help over losing the flat. Not being able to advise her son was what upset her most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives sensible people time to get ready. I'd tell the apprentices to add the new skills on top of the old ones. I'd tell Yusuf the same thing, louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. If Northgate trains me to run the new machines, I could stay on in some form. Yusuf has time to get out of the taxi before it's worthless, and Bilal can steer his training towards the robot side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools as soon as the first few people had, and ask Northgate straight out to train me. I'd make Yusuf sell the taxi in the next two or three years and find steadier work, maybe driving for the council. And I'd talk to Bilal about adding a course in machine controls on top of his electrical ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Changing Bilal's training is a big decision. How would he take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably like it, actually, he's always been into gadgets. It's me who'd be nervous, because I believe in a solid trade. But a solid trade in 2031 might mean fixing the robots, and I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make Yusuf sell the taxi. Is that your decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's ours, but I'd push hard. He's the head of the house and I respect that. But I do the sums, and the sums would say sell while someone still wants to buy.

S3.say: Five years gives sensible people time to get ready. I'd tell the apprentices, and my husband even louder, to add new skills on top of old ones.
S3.think: By 63, if Northgate trains me on the new machines, I could stay on. My husband has time to get out of the taxi and my son can steer his training towards robots.
S3.do: Learns new tools once the first few have and asks Northgate directly for training. Pushes her husband to sell the taxi within two or three years and find steadier work, and encourages her son to add a machine-controls course to his electrical training.
S3.quote: But a solid trade in 2031 might mean fixing the robots, and I can live with that.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan for the whole household: her own training, her husband's exit from taxi work and her son's course. She respects her husband as head of the house but does the sums herself. Her belief in a solid trade bends to include fixing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to train a whole new generation properly, so let's do apprenticeships right. I'd say that at work and to anyone who asked. I'd not say the government should pay people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd be out of it. But Bilal would be 31, right in the middle of his working life, and that's what keeps me up. I spent my life telling him a trade was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northgate and save a little more now the loan would be gone. I'd sit down with Bilal this year and plan his next ten years properly, which certificates, which firms, whether to move to the city for the robot work. I'd keep training Ellie and Jordan and tell them the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for Bilal. For myself it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you told him a trade was safe. Do you regret that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I meant it, and it was true for me. But I'd be telling him something different now, and I'd have to admit I was wrong. That's not easy for a mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Bilal moved to the city for robot work, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like losing him a bit. We're a family that eats together on Fridays. But I'd rather he had work in the city than nothing here. I'd make the drive.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to train a new generation properly, so let's do apprenticeships right. The government shouldn't pay people to sit at home.
S4.think: I'd be 68 and out of it, but my son would be 31 and in the middle of his working life. I spent my life telling him a trade was safe.
S4.do: Keeps working at Northgate and saves more once the taxi loan is gone. Sits down with her son this year to plan his next ten years, including certificates, firms and a possible move to the city, and keeps training her apprentices.
S4.feel: Anxious for her son, fine for herself.
S4.quote: I spent my life telling him a trade was safe.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her own job is safe enough, but her worry moves fully onto her son, who would be mid-career. She feels responsible for having told him a trade was safe. She stays anxious because her sense of herself as a mother is tied to his security.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it hits Yusuf, Bilal and me all at once. What would help is if firms like Northgate trained their own loyal people first, and if apprenticeships were changed fast enough that young ones like Bilal learn the new work, not just the old. I'd rather a hand up than a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. I've been the only woman on most sites for thirty-odd years, and Ellie's the first girl apprentice I've had. I'd hate for her to fight her way in just as the door closes.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for her to fight her way in just as the door closes.
portrait: Iris Khan is a 58-year-old site joiner on apartment blocks for the only big builder in her town, who hangs fire doors, mentors two apprentices and checks fire rules on an AI app now and then. She has three weeks of savings, a husband driving a taxi on a loan and a son in an electrical apprenticeship she's proud of. She's calm in the Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, mostly about her husband's taxi. AGI by 2028 alarms her because all three of them would be hit at once, and with five or ten years she plans for her household, ending anxious about her son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her husband, her son and her all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Firms training their loyal workers first, and apprenticeships changed quickly enough to teach young people the new work.
